title: The Joint Programme
logline: You are Anna Kovač's lawyer. She's a young logistics coordinator at Kade Freight — the import firm from Week 1's case, grown into a small pan-EU carrier — who was refused a six-month exchange to the Malta office. She's found a line in the Treaties that seems to promise her a way through. Tonight the Groningen District Court's Employment & EU Law Chamber decides two things: whether that Treaty line can bind her employer at all, and whether the EU regulation that might have made it bite was ever legally taken off the table.
learning_goal: By the end, the player can: 1. Apply the combined Van Gend & Loos + Defrenne II test for direct horizontal effect of a Treaty provision, and recognise that a provision must first pass the Van Gend & Loos requirements (clear, unconditional) before Defrenne II's extra requirement (mandatory in nature, suitable to operate between individuals) is even reached [L2 p.4], [L2 p.9], [L2 p.10], [WA2 p.1]. 2. State how legislative power is split between Parliament, Council, the European Council and the Commission, and why only the Commission normally has the legislative initiative [L2 p.13], [L2 p.14], [L2 p.16], [WA2 p.1]. 3. Distinguish the ordinary legislative procedure (OLP, Article 294 TFEU) from a special legislative procedure (SLP), and a legislative act from a non-legislative act, delegated act or implementing act [L2 p.18], [L2 p.19], [L2 p.20], [L2 p.23], [L2 p.28], [L2 p.29], [WA2 p.1]. 4. Apply the three requirements from Council v Commission (C-409/13) for a valid withdrawal of a Commission legislative proposal, in the right order [L2 p.39], [L2 p.41], [WG2b p.16]. 5. Avoid the "typical errors": omitting to apply the Van Gend & Loos requirements to the actual wording of the provision; omitting Defrenne II; reaching for the wrong Treaty article (e.g. free movement of workers) instead of the one actually in the hypothetical; and treating the Commission's power to withdraw as either an absolute veto or as something the Treaties simply forbid [WA2 p.1], [L2 p.35].

quiz.question: Anna relies on Article 47 TFEU ("Member States shall, within the framework of a joint programme, encourage the exchange of young workers") against her employer, Kade Freight. No such joint programme currently exists. Does Anna have a right under EU law that this court must protect?

options.text: No. Article 47 TFEU is not sufficiently clear and precise, and it is conditional on a joint programme that does not yet exist, so it needs further implementation by EU or national law. It fails the Van Gend & Loos requirements for direct effect, so the Defrenne II question of horizontal effect never has to be reached.
Yes. Article 119 EEC (now Article 157 TFEU) shows that Treaty provisions can bind private employers, and Defrenne II is exactly this kind of case: an individual against a private company.
options.story: the lawyer sketches Sabena's logo next to Kade Freight's on a legal pad. Haan doesn't even stand to object. "Counsel, you've shown me a horizontal-effect case. You haven't shown me a direct-effect one."
options.teaching: Defrenne II's extra requirement only matters once Van Gend & Loos's clarity and unconditionality are already satisfied. Citing Defrenne II without first testing the provision's own wording is a typical error the model answer specifically warns against [WA2 p.1], [L2 p.10].

options.text: Yes. Article 45 TFEU on free movement of workers requires Member States to remove obstacles to workers moving between Member States, and Kade Freight's refusal is such an obstacle.
options.story: Haan slides the TFEU's table of contents across the bench. "Counsel, there's more than one article on workers."
options.teaching: Article 45 TFEU concerns free movement of workers generally; Anna's claim is built on Article 47 TFEU specifically, the exchange-of-young-workers provision. Reaching for a different, more familiar Treaty article instead of the one the hypothetical actually gives you is a typical student error, especially for provisions students already studied elsewhere [WA2 p.1].

options.text: No. Article 47 TFEU addresses only "Member States", so it can never bind Kade Freight, a private company.
options.story: Judge De Wit almost nods — then stops. "That's not why it fails, Counsel."
options.teaching: That a provision names "Member States" as the addressee does not by itself rule out horizontal effect — Defrenne II shows the opposite is possible. Article 47 TFEU fails because it is conditional on a joint programme that does not exist, not because of who it names. Reaching the right conclusion by skipping the actual Van Gend & Loos test scores no application credit [WA2 p.1], [SA p.5].

irac.issue: Does Article 47 TFEU create a right for Anna, enforceable against Kade Freight, a private employer? Because the claim runs against a private party, this is a question of direct horizontal effect [L2 p.4], [WA2 p.1].
irac.rule: A Treaty provision has direct effect only if it is (1) clear and (2) unconditional, i.e. it needs no further implementation by EU or national law (Van Gend & Loos). Only if both are met does the further question arise whether the provision is (3) mandatory in nature and suitable, content-wise, to operate between private parties (Defrenne II) [L2 p.9], [L2 p.10], [WA2 p.1].
irac.application: Article 47 TFEU obliges Member States to encourage the exchange of young workers "within the framework of a joint programme". Whether the wording is clear enough is arguable either way, but its unconditionality is not: the provision expressly depends on a "joint programme", and no such programme exists yet. Without it, neither the age limits for "young" workers nor the specific conduct required of anyone is determined. The provision therefore needs further implementation and is conditional [WA2 p.1], [WG2 p.3]. Because Van Gend & Loos's requirements are not met, it is not necessary to go on and ask whether the obligation is also suitable to bind a private employer under Defrenne II [WA2 p.1].
irac.conclusion: Article 47 TFEU does not have direct effect. Anna has no right against Kade Freight under this provision [WA2 p.1].

dialogue.speaker: HAAN

dialogue.speaker: JUDGE DE WIT
dialogue.line: Is it, Counsel? Was this withdrawal even valid?

Lawyer reading the exhibit, tracing the dates with a finger

shots.subject: Judge De Wit: "Was this withdrawal even valid?" → EXAMINATION II

quiz.question: The Commission proposed the "Youth Bridge" Regulation. The Council formally adopted its position accepting Parliament's amendment on Tuesday. On Wednesday, the Commission withdrew the proposal, stating in writing that the amendment (requiring unanimous Council sign-off for every national quota) distorted the proposal's purpose. Was the withdrawal valid?

options.text: Yes, because the Commission always has an unconditional right to withdraw its own legislative proposal — the proposal belongs to the institution that wrote it.
options.story: Haan smiles, folder still raised — then the case-file HUD flags the claim in sodium-amber and freezes.
options.teaching: The CJEU expressly rejected this: a power of withdrawal that could be exercised at will "would confer... a right of veto in the conduct of the legislative process," contrary to the principles of conferral of powers and institutional balance [L2 p.35]. The Commission's power is conditional on all three requirements, not unconditional.

options.text: Yes, because the Commission stated detailed, written grounds, supported by evidence, for the withdrawal.
options.story: the lawyer starts to nod along with Haan's written grounds — then stops, re-reading the exhibit's dates. "Tuesday. You withdrew on Wednesday."
options.teaching: Stating cogent grounds is the second requirement, but it never gets reached if the first requirement — that the Council has not yet acted — already fails. The three requirements must be checked in the order the Court gave them; good grounds cannot rescue a withdrawal that came too late [L2 p.39], [L2 p.41].

options.text: No, because the Council had already acted — it had formally adopted its position — before the Commission withdrew the proposal.
No, because the Treaties never mention a power to withdraw a proposal at all, only a power to alter it.
options.story: Judge De Wit tilts her head: "So the Commission never had the power at all?"
options.teaching: Article 293(2) TFEU is silent on withdrawal, mentioning only alteration — but the CJEU read Article 17(2) TEU together with Articles 289 TFEU and 293 TFEU to establish a new rule: the Commission does have a power to withdraw, subject to the three requirements. Treaty silence on withdrawal does not mean withdrawal is always unlawful; it means the CJEU had to work out the conditions under which it is lawful [L2 p.34], [L2 p.39]. In this hypothetical the withdrawal is invalid regardless — but for the timing reason (C), not because the power doesn't exist.

irac.issue: Did the Commission validly withdraw the "Youth Bridge" proposal, given that the Council had already adopted its position accepting Parliament's amendment? [L2 p.41]
irac.rule: Council v Commission (C-409/13): the Commission's power to withdraw a legislative proposal is not a veto and is subject to three requirements, which must be checked in order: (1) the Council must not yet have acted; (2) the Commission must state to Parliament and Council the grounds for withdrawal, supported by cogent evidence or arguments; (3) the Commission may withdraw only after having due regard to the concerns of Parliament and Council, in the spirit of sincere cooperation [L2 p.39], [L2 p.41], [WG2b p.16]. Article 293(2) TFEU expressly allows the Commission to alter its proposal "as long as the Council has not acted" — the same time limit governs withdrawal [L2 p.32], [L2 p.34].
irac.application: Here the Council formally adopted its position on Tuesday, before the Commission withdrew the proposal on Wednesday. The first requirement — that the Council must not yet have acted — is not met. It therefore makes no difference that the Commission's stated grounds might otherwise have been cogent (the second requirement) or that it had considered Parliament's and Council's concerns (the third requirement): the first requirement fails, and that is decisive [L2 p.41], [WG2b p.16].
irac.conclusion: The withdrawal of the "Youth Bridge" proposal was invalid. The Council had already acted.

dialogue.line: On the claim before me tonight: dismissed. Article 47 TFEU gives Ms Kovač no right this court can protect, for want of a joint programme. case_file: Claimant: Anna Kovač, logistics coordinator, Kade Freight Logistics B.V.
Claim: a right to a 6-month exchange to Kade Freight's Malta office under a Treaty provision on the exchange of young workers.
Respondent's exhibit flagged: an EU Commission withdrawal of a related legislative proposal.

irac.issue: Does Anna Kovač have a right against Kade Freight under Article 47 TFEU?
irac.rule: Van Gend & Loos (clear, unconditional) + Defrenne II (mandatory in nature, suitable between private parties) [L2 p.9], [L2 p.10].
irac.application: Article 47 TFEU is conditional on a "joint programme" that does not exist; unconditionality fails; Defrenne II is not reached [WA2 p.1].
irac.conclusion: No direct effect. Anna has no right against Kade Freight today [WA2 p.1].

irac.issue: Was the Commission's withdrawal of the "Youth Bridge" proposal valid?
irac.rule: Council v Commission (C-409/13): three requirements, checked in order — Council not yet acted; grounds stated with cogent evidence; due regard to Parliament's and Council's concerns [L2 p.39], [L2 p.41].
irac.application: The Council had already adopted its position before the Commission withdrew; the first requirement fails [L2 p.41].
irac.conclusion: The withdrawal was invalid — the "Youth Bridge" file is, on this record, still legally pending.

verdict.takeaway: "A Treaty provision that depends on a programme that doesn't exist yet has no direct effect — vertical or horizontal — until that programme is adopted. And a withdrawn EU proposal isn't dead just because someone says it is: check whether the Council had already acted."

checks.claim: Van Gend & Loos only answered whether a Treaty provision creates rights against the State (vertical); it left open whether a provision can bind another individual (horizontal)

In 1976, Defrenne II established that a clear and unconditional Treaty provision may create rights enforceable against another individual — "direct horizontal effect"; "individuals" covers all private parties
Article 119 EEC (equal pay) is now Article 157 TFEU
Defrenne facts: Sabena air hostess, automatic dismissal at 40, no anti-discrimination Directives at the time; Defrenne I (1971, pension excluded from "pay"); Defrenne II, Case 43/75, 8 April 1976

Article 119 is unconditional for direct/overt discrimination (identifiable from the article alone) but conditional for indirect/disguised discrimination (needs implementing provisions) — paras 18, 21, 22
Para 39: Article 119 is mandatory in nature and extends to collective agreements and contracts between individuals; para 40: it may be relied on before national courts, which must protect it
Exam method: first apply Van Gend & Loos (clear, unconditional), then Defrenne II (mandatory in nature, suitable to operate between individuals)
The Commission has no legislative power but has the legislative initiative; Article 17(2) TEU; Article 289(4) TFEU (other initiators in specific cases)
Parliament, Council, or one million citizens may request the Commission to submit a proposal: Articles 225, 241 TFEU, Article 11(4) TEU
Article 289 TFEU: OLP = joint adoption by Parliament + Council on a Commission proposal (Art. 294); SLP = adoption by one with the participation of the other, in specific cases
Article 294 TFEU steps: proposal, first reading (no deadline), second reading (3 months), conciliation (6 weeks), third reading (6 weeks)
Example SLP: Article 21(3) TFEU (Council unanimity after consulting Parliament)
Article 288 TFEU: regulations (general, binding entirely, directly applicable), directives (binding as to result, form/methods left to MS), decisions (binding entirely, may specify addressees)
Article 289(3) TFEU: it is the procedure, not the type of act, that makes an act legislative or non-legislative
Non-legislative procedure example for executive-type measures: Article 43(3) TFEU (fixing prices); historical-reasons example: Article 103(1) TFEU
Article 297 TFEU: legislative acts published in the OJ, enter into force on the date specified or the 20th day after publication; some directives/decisions instead take effect on notification
Delegated acts: Article 290 TFEU — Commission may supplement/amend non-essential elements of a legislative act; conditions must be explicit; Parliament/Council may revoke or object
Implementing acts: Article 291 TFEU — uniform conditions for implementing binding Union acts, powers conferred on the Commission (or, in specific cases, the Council)

Council v Commission (C-409/13) facts: 2011 Commission proposal on macro-financial assistance under Articles 209/212 TFEU; Article 7 conferred implementing powers on the Commission; Council + Parliament wanted OLP for each MFA decision instead; Commission withdrew
Article 293(2) TFEU allows the Commission to alter its proposal "as long as the Council has not acted"; alteration is not the same as withdrawal
Council's action for annulment (Articles 263-264 TFEU); three pleas: conferral/institutional balance, sincere cooperation (Art. 13(2) TEU), obligation to state reasons (Art. 296(2) TFEU)
Para 64: institutional balance (not new); para 74: Article 17(2) TEU with Articles 289 + 293 TFEU gives the Commission power to alter or withdraw
Para 75: the power of withdrawal cannot amount to a right of veto — contrary to conferral of powers and institutional balance

The three requirements for valid withdrawal: (1) Council has not acted (para 74); (2) grounds stated with cogent evidence (para 76); (3) due regard to Parliament's/Council's concerns, in sincere cooperation (para 83) — and confirmed independently
All three of the Council's pleas were rejected as unfounded (para 108); the withdrawal in the real case was lawful because all three requirements were met
2016 Interinstitutional Agreement on Better Law-Making — a non-legislative act, Article 295 TFEU
IRAC method: Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion, applied one requirement at a time
Article 4(3) TEU (sincere cooperation) and Article 13(2) TEU (institutional balance)
Article 47 TFEU text: "Member States shall, within the framework of a joint programme, encourage the exchange of young workers"

The Anna case: young worker, employer refuses an exchange, provision fails clarity/unconditionality because the "joint programme" does not exist, so direct effect (and therefore horizontal effect) is not established

Typical student errors: omitting to apply the requirements to the provision's wording; omitting to cite Van Gend & Loos; omitting to cite Defrenne II; wrongly reaching for free movement of workers (Article 45 TFEU) instead of the provision actually given
Exam grading splits marks into knowledge and application

coordinator_notes: N1: One rank-1 WG file misstates the holding of Council v Commission. This does not match the lecture, which is unambiguous that C-409/13 is about the Commission's power to withdraw a legislative proposal [L2 p.31-p.41], and it does not match the alternate WG file, International and European Law WG Week 2.pdf p.16, which gives the correct withdrawal-power account. This game follows the lecture and the correctly-aligned WG file, and does not use European Law WG Week 2.pdf pages 9, 10 or 12 for anything about this case.
